title: Aron Pietroń, Michał Ogłoziński - Discussion (Against the Storm)
speaker: Aron Pietroń, Michał Ogłoziński
description: Host Alexei Pepers and developers Aron Pietroń and Michał Ogłoziński of Eremite Games will discuss the development of their Roguelite citybuilder Against the Storm.

segments.text: >> Hi. ALEXEI: Welcoming Aron
and Michal of Emrites Games. Doing proper introductions. Aron is a co-founder and
is the producer of Against the Storm. His previous work on dying light two and dying
light bad blood taught him how to create scalable products which benefit the early
access growth of Against the Storm. When not making games he is playing with his puppies
and relentlessly trying to convince Michal that gothic is a better game than morian.
And Michal another co-founder of Emrites Games -- puts the past experience working on live service
games into practice by releasing new Against the Storm content updates every two weeks.
Very fast. >> Thank you for having
us tonight. Hello from across the Atlantic. >> Yes, it is always wonderful when we can get
people from a little further away than the usual San Francisco locale. Thank you for working with
our time zones. >>
It has been fun. Hi. We've played some games before hopping on the
stream. So we had a long night. ALEXEI: Excellent. Well, yeah,
to get into it, I think that, you know, maybe actually, hopefully, people have played Against
the Storm but if not, if you want to talk about it and the most interesting thing to
us is the roguelite citybuilder connection and how you got to that combination which is
interesting and one that works extremely well. I have played a lot of Against the
Storm in the last week. I will tell you that. >> Maybe Aron can kickoff and talk about the
game itself and I can continue with the roguelike elements.
>> Yeah. Let's go with that. So for those of you who haven't played Against the Storm
it is a game that takes the citybuilder core of all the mechanics of the player's actions
and spices them up with roguelike/roguelite elements. When we designed Against the Storm
from the beginning we tried to distill the essence of our citybuilder of the beginning
1-2 hours of gameplay loop in the citybuilder. We focused mostly on the repairability side and the
generation side of roguelites and we took those elements, implemented them into the game and the
game is out on Steam right now. It has been almost two years of early access biweekly updates and a
lot of player feedback so the game is evolving still. That's being a roguelite is helpful in that
because we changed the balance here and there. The game is heavily reliant on RNG, of course,
so we know tuning that and giving players new content results in basically a lot of
replayability. One of the main, I think, draws to the game is we have like a perk system, blueprints
for buildings which are generated so you never play the same hand, you have something of random,
pseudo random hand you are dealt, and you have to find ways of playing with it basically.
And the game is like cut in some smaller like sessions where you build a city for
two hours and then you move on to the world map where you find another way to settle somewhere
and you start this loop again. Then, of course, the game is progressively getting harder the more
you play and there is also roguelite elements come into play. That's why we call it roguelite because
we have permanent progression there that you can buy in the main City of the game basically.
I don't know if you, Michal, want to add something to the roguelike element here.
>> Sure. I think you heard this discussion but just to be sure, for us, like when we thought
about it initially, the roguelite is more of an RPG elements is the same basically. You can have
RPG elements and a farming game with RPG elements. We thought he could capture the same feeling with
roguelikes. We have built a very simple prototype of a simple citybuilder and then we thought OK,
if a roguelike is just like an element of RPG, how does it manifest? What does it mean for a game to
be a roguelike? What do we need? So we identified a few elements. For example, the most important
for us was the power fund -- sorry. Ultimate power fund. This ability in roguelikes and roguelites
and you play to find this one magical build 1 time out of 20 and absolutely break the game and in any
other generate would be unacceptable. It would be boring and just one strategy to play but in this
one magical generates it is actually what we do. That was one of the elements to the decisions and
the meaningful repercussions of those decisions was very important to us. Also,
the cycle, the roguelikes have very unique beats about them. You can play them for two
hours and leave them to return after two weeks and play eight hours or whatever
and leave the game for another month. We enjoyed that and felt it is great thing to
find a way into the citybuilder generator which is great. We love it. But we thought that we can
breathe a bit of life to genre that is getting stalled maybe. It was much easier to think that
way. Those are the elements. Those are like flavors. Let's put it into a citybuilder.
ALEXEI: That's really
interesting in the way that with roguelites you can push what a really good combination
looks like and also what a really bad combination because worst case you will fail the run but there
will be another one right after and that's interesting in comparison -- I like how
especially I find at the beginning of a game of a citybuilder you often end up with a pattern that
you do every single time because that's kind of optimal but there are so many conditions
that change in Against the Storm because of the roguelike elements that will make you push what
you do and you have to restrategize every time. >> That is something that we struggled with.
Almost every change we implement into the game was measured in a way does it help replayability,
does it make run different between each other? And if the feature didn't make the game different,
even if it was fantastic, in most cases, we didn't go for it. We thought very hard about
what could make players play differently basically. That's something that as you mentioned
it is not -- it is quite unique in citybuilder. ALEXEI:
Yeah, were there any examples where you found something that seemed like a good idea but didn't
help with that replayability? How drew test that? Think through? Or is that one where the speed of
your updates help and seeing how the community plays with the new update? Do you take things out
if it isn't impacting the replayability? >> There are multiple steps
to be honest. The first one is the designer in his head and to be honest there were many ideas that
we as designers think are great but then when we slip it in the look at the screen on another
day we can clearly see it is a bad idea. The second feature is the team itself. We are really
believing in democrucized project and all decide if the future is worth it or not -- feature. I
can give an example from like last month that I thought about would be great system, like
city is having walls because walls look fantastic and they would breathe a lot of life to the game,
but on the very first stage Aron was like I don't think that will make -- like in every game players
will feel obliged to do it and every town will look the same and there will just be another
action you have to complete in another game and to be honest that was enough because he
was right. If you would add such an overwhelmingly impactful system to the game it would be repeated
in every game and defeat the purpose. But also, as you said, the next filter is the players
themselves. I don't think there are many occasions where we cut the feature entirely but there are
multiple examples of features that we iterated like three or four times before we settled on a
version that both we and the players enjoyed and thought it helped their playability.
I don't know about an example. >> Not sure about an example but
I think even if we focus very heavily on creating replayability and creating difference experiences
between different runs we still have some small actions in the game or some points where it's
unavoidable to an extent. Like in an action game, in a turn-base game, those actions are so
small that you don't really nets them. -- notice them. In a citybuilder, your basic actions are a
lot longer and their time span is longer. For example, in our game, most sessions start with
you build up some roads for your city. You build up wood camp. You build up a gathering camp. These
are the basic actions that basically happen every time. Sometimes you do them in a different order
but they are sometimes the same. It is always a bit of that repeated action there. But also
I think that when miMichal was talk about the last filter, which are the players,
one very good tool we were using for filtering those repeatable and not so interesting mechanics
is we do experimental branch. We do biweekly updates but when we have something controversial
to add and aren't sure ourselves if it is the best idea we just give the most dedicated players
access to a beta branch basically and they can test the new feature and give us feedback.
We always ask like pointed questions in those beta stages. We ask one of the most important
questions there is always like how does this feature or this change influence the gameplay
over all? Is the gameplay more boring or repeatable? Or is it more interesting?
I can't think of any other like big features that we cut lately. There has been a lot of features.
Yeah. I think that's all that we can think of on that topic.
ALEXEI: Yeah, and then it is interesting that, you know, element of getting information from
the community. Travis asked what kind of metrics do you collect? Do you get things
like the average game time from players? What difficulty they are on? What kind of information
have you found helpful to collect there? >> Our background is actually like mobile
games so we are a bit skewed. -- in that sense. We really enjoy going, of course anonymous analytics
like gameplay analytics and going through it with like every basically two weeks in some form. But
of course that's only small part of the picture. Like there are so many occasions in which the
data is pointing in one direction. Even like the simplest examples like havingperks and you look
at the percentage of perks being picked and even just looking at the numbers can be very misleading
because very often the most interesting and beloved perks are also the most situational
and they won't be picked that often. They are completely fine and we don't want to change them.
But looking at the numbers themselves you could say here is the most boring perk every made and it
is most -- we have this one that's actually 50% to wood cutting speed and it is horrible but we can't
convince the community that it's not. It is always there in the top. So we gather a lot of analytics
but we don't go blindly into it. We really read the feedback on all of the channels that we can
put our hands-on. Maybe those days, nowadays, we don't have that much time and sometimes we miss
a thing or two but we really focus on that. I think it is crucial for our like process.
Aron probably could have summarized it better. >> With analytics we have the most basic ones like
the perks that people choose, the buildings they choose because this is also generated.
The basic actions they take in a game. The events they encounter and how do they solve
them. So these are like as Michal said it is helping us create a good balance background
so for example because those spiky perks as Michal said are the most interesting ones but
they have to be juxtapose to a background that's balanced. That helps us with that.
There is also like the issue of scale a bit because before you have a game released it is
hard to get feedback because nobody really cares about the game. When you have the game released
now and people are playing it daily then the feedback is almost overwhelming to a degree.
It is also, aside from pick thing right feedback from the analytics -- picking -- we monitor the
YouTube channels, disorder messages, Reddit and Team forums and so on.
Our duty is to basically read everything but we also have to correctly filter it because between
the lines, between the feedback, there is a lot of feedback that is saying something else that
is written. For example, people wanting some perks or some abilities or anything to be more
powerful doesn't really mean that something is like not -- is too weak or not really fun.
Sometimes it is just because that's their favorite play style and they want to have even more power
tied to it. So we have to be careful witht at a. -- with that. I have this problem where I try to
reactively change stuff in the game because when there is player feedback there has to be something
wrong but that's not always the case. I think we slowed down with the feedback a bit because
of the scale but always because of the scale -- also -- and there sea of feedback you can see
the points more clearly. The best thing about balance for example is balance if people talk
about it from both sides and argue it is the best because then there is no clear answer and that's
a fun thing to witness because, you know, talking about balance is something we as gamers enjoy.
ALEXEI: It is great point. I have heard the advice before when someone says they have a
problem usually that's true. And then they say here is the solution and that's when
you know you need to take a minute and think about if that's actually the best solution.
>> Yeah, we also use like this special site for example in React called up vote where people can
post their feature requests, their balance requests, and so on. It is very good tool
to collect and collect up-votes for different like feature requests from players. But it is
also a tool where you have to be careful with the solutions as you said because people offer
a lot of solutions for things that they think should change in the game but a lot of the time
the solutions are somewhere else. It is not that this perk for example is weak. It is maybe that
this play style is not really well defined and it should have more definition before we change the
perks that are tied to it and so on and so on. So it is always a bit of a guessing game and also a
bit of -- yeah. Reading between the lines. >> I just wanted to add that maybe I am a
bit -- or we are a bit freaked out about player feedback but we always talked about
players have the full right in our opinion to write convoluted and emotional feedback,
to write just blatantly wrong feedback, whatever. It is like -- it is not
their job to give perfect informed and designed well thoughtful feedback because
we really believe that that's something that the designer is responsible for. Like we need
to look at this -- sometimes emotional ranting. Especially in games like ours when there is like
the stakes can be high. People can get emotional sometimes. I must admit we have
communities -- it is not like league of legends or something. We all know it. But I truly believe
it is our job as designers to unpack it, to really get to the bottom of the feedback.
ALEXEI: And I wanted to ask because Aron you mentioned at one point the need to resist the
urge to get too caught up in the feedback and kind of be reactive. Have you found
any good techniques to help especially there is sometimes that emotional toll if you are hearing
emotionally charged feedback. How do you take that in in a way that stops you from being too
reactive or getting too stressed out? It is a lot of work and can be overwhelming
especially negative or emotional feedback. >> Probably the best advice is waiting two weeks.
There are multiple occasions where people are like it is horrible and after a week or two
people get used to it. And not in a bad way. In like oh, yeah, it is horrible but now I can
live with that. More like after they play with it a bit they find a way to basically
implement it into their play style, for example, to use this mechanic, to basically win with it,
or just find a niche for it. In many cases that's the time that's the factor that we need.
>> Yeah, because of the time we can judge if this change was influencing the play style in
a good way because we want to sometimes disrupt the player's play style a bit especially if the
game has such a long lifetime or if it is just a bad design and people universally hate it. I
think the other tool that's very useful, not very useful for solo devs, but a team it is useful. We
basically talk about it a lot. And for example, I am a bit more reactive but Michal is a bit
more level headed, so we find common ground there when it comes to addressing feedback.
Luke our community manager is very player centered so even if we have an urge to
dismiss or not dismiss feedback but say let's wait with that it will be fine in two days we
still have this itch from the team to respond to that and take into consideration and makes it in.
Being in a team of different individuals is helping with that and coping with the
feedback especially if the emotional one which somebody takes emotional feedback too serious
and too hard. Then the rest can console them. ALEXEI: You mentioned a couple times the longer
cycle which is something I found interesting. A citybuilder with the way it is broken and runs has
a longer feel than a typical roguelike does. I am curious how some of that came into it and Travis
asked a question about the queens impatience bar something that mechanically forces the player's
speed and you have to end up completing by a certain time and was that a thematic choice
or coming from mechanically needing a way to limit how long a run is? How do you think about
the time a run takes when you bring in those roguelike elements which are a little faster?
>> I think early on in the project we were thinking about how long the session could
possibly be and very quickly we came to the like hour and a half and two hours so we were always
designing the game to be so the runs would be as long. Every major positive change was always the
balance to make the game shorter or longer. The queens impatience for us was very important in the
project. We publuxed a demo on steam one year into production. -- published. The game was in a rough
state. It was playable and people had fun but it was very simplistic. The queens impatience was a
timer basically. Nowadays it is more of a resource and you can stretch it, reduce it, increase it,
there are benefits to having it but back in the day it was 30 minutes or one hour time out. It
is horrible. Like one of the worst mechanics in the game. People should be upset about it.
We didn't have time to implement anything more interesting because when you race with time it
doesn't sound that fun. But we put like a very fantasy taste of a queen that's very impatient. It
matches expectations. You can see her. I remember watching the first few streams that someone posted
and he was screaming like please. I knew it was 24 minutes out of 25. There is absolutely nothing.
Like behind this thin layer of fiction. It was enough for players. I remember I was stunned by
how much one can achieve and just a thin layer of friction that matches the expectation because if
that would be I don't know -- >>
Oh, we lost Michal. >>
He is logging back in. >> The queen just cut him off because he was
saying bad stuff about her. No, but you had some early problems with that. We had early problems
with that when we first pitched the idea to publishers. We talked about feedback from outside
the team in the early days before the demo even. We encountered an issue from the beginning that
this is just a timer and that some people even today when they buy the game on Steam and play it
like they would a normal citybuilder they still feel like this is the expectation. They want to
play a longer game. They don't want to be rushed. That's a raiment where I think we manage to create
more of a resource out of it. -- moment. It is decreased because you have reputation. We want
more sometimes because it lowers the possibility of the forest. It is now more mechanic than a
timer but even to this day there is some people who don't really like that but that's something
we want to really address because the game has an identity right now. It is roguelike
citybuilder. That's one of the elements. And some pressure. There has to be some pressure. We can
>> I will note there is a negative thing that is controlling how long can you play
but also there is a positive thing. When you are doing great, every species very happy,
the game is done. Completed quickly. Like a minute or two. It is also very like intentional decision.
We don't want the player to be satisfied for too long. It is like -- it is very
I would say blaming like if you are having a perfect build you are just going to absolutely
demolish everything you encounter and that's great. But the game cannot give you too much of
this power because otherwise you would just get bored with a regular game and like a very thin
ice I would say. We need to step on as project designers. It is like controlled on both sides.
ALEXEI: I think a question that can be fun is are there any particular favorite fun stories you have
had either seeing people achieve combinations in the game you didn't expect or if you know when
you were testing things you had an idea that when you went into it created some situation
that was unexpected like some favorite moments? >> We routinely get screen shots from players when
they break a record in resource gathering. That's one of the measures of success in citybuilder.
Your economy is like your power measure in the game a bit.
So we routinely get some screen shots where somebody has like 50,000 meet and there are
some perks used to get to that because we have perks that the more you produce the more you gain
in the next production cycle plus you get meat when somebody dies and you get a perk that doesn't
increase the queen's impatience because normally it grows when somebody dies in the village.
There is a perk that disables that. They give them meat if somebody dies. They trigger hostile events
to kill people off and gather more resources but I can't think of anything crazier than
that. I don't know if you have anything. >> There was one thing where we had an event
called living matter and it was an event that was slowly chewing your food. And if
you wouldn't solve it, it would like duplicate and stay on the map. Now we have two and they
will duplicate to four. If you thought it is a great event. Well, if you want to solve it,
and it had some really good rewards and you could farm T. You had to be careful. You forget about
them or won't have resources to fix them and everything will spiral out of control
and destroy privilege on a wonderful design. But there players of course find a way to stop
it. They were building like those small fences around four of them. They were like creating
a small farm of living matter just because -- we want it to be cool. The event was avoiding
any buildings or structures so not to destroy anything. The players were using it to farm the
living matter for like the entirety of the game. >> Yeah because you could basically enclose it in
a small fence and the game would then say I don't have space to duplicate so I am going to stay
here and they just use that to create an enclosure for the living matter, yeah.
ALEXEI: Did you decide to leave it that way? Or fix it?
>> No, no. It destroyed buildings, no. ALEXEI:
I love -- only in roguelikes can you get away with having those exponential every
time you do this this happens and the loops but they can go too far.
Well, excellent. Yeah, I know we gave a little extra time because we started late
but we should let you go. It has been wonderful to have you here. It is great when we can have
people from the other side of the ocean and I am excited, yeah, for more people hopefully in
the roguelike community if they didn't know to try it out. I think the roguelike citybuilder
concept just worked so well. It is great to see the game keeps changing so quickly that
there is always new stuff to check out. >> Thank you very much. Yeah. We will keep
updating the game probably this year at the end of the year it is going to be out of early
access so it is going to be a bit less chaotic and balance wise you don't have to relearn it
every two weeks maybe. We will see about that.
Yeah. It is going to be fun. Yeah. Thank you very much for the talk.
>> Thank you for having us. Yeah. It was great talking to you.
